warmup.q: A coroutine launched on Dispatchers.Default calls a blocking JDBC query that takes 300 ms. The pod has 4 cores. What does that call cost the rest of the service while it runs?
options: Nothing: a coroutine suspends while the query runs, so the thread is free
One of the 4 Default threads is stuck for 300 ms, so other CPU work queues behind it
Nothing: kotlinx.coroutines moves blocking calls to Dispatchers.IO by itself
The call fails, because blocking calls are not allowed in a coroutine
warmup.why: A coroutine only frees its thread at a suspension point, and a JDBC call is not one: it blocks the thread. Default has one thread per core, so on 4 cores, four such calls stop all CPU work. Nothing detects or moves the call for you. You move it with withContext(Dispatchers.IO).

sections.h: A dispatcher picks the thread, and withContext switches it
sections.html:
suspend says nothing about threads (lesson 1 of this track). The dispatcher in a coroutine's context does: it decides which thread runs the coroutine each time it starts or resumes. kotlinx.coroutines ships four.

  • Dispatchers.Default is a pool with one thread per CPU core, and at least two. launch and async use it when the context names no dispatcher.
  • Dispatchers.IO is for calls that block a thread, such as JDBC or a blocking HTTP client. Up to 64 of them run at once.
  • Dispatchers.Main is the UI thread on Android, JavaFX or Swing, and needs a UI module on the classpath. A Quarkus service has none, and using it throws IllegalStateException.
  • Dispatchers.Unconfined has no thread of its own. The coroutine starts on the caller's thread and, after its first suspension, carries on on whatever thread resumed it. The docs say it should not be used in general code.

runBlocking is the odd one out: it runs its coroutine on the thread that called it.

To run one piece of work somewhere else, use withContext:

Java
// Java equivalent: CompletableFuture stages, each with its own executor
CompletableFuture<byte[]> statementPdf(String accountId) {
    return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> store.loadRows(accountId), ioPool)  // blocking JDBC call
        .thenApplyAsync(renderer::render, cpuPool);                                // CPU-heavy layout
}
Kotlin
suspend fun statementPdf(accountId: String): ByteArray {
    val rows = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { store.loadRows(accountId) }   // blocking JDBC call
    return withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { renderer.render(rows) }      // CPU-heavy layout
}

withContext suspends the caller, runs the block on the other dispatcher, and then resumes the caller on its own dispatcher with the block's result. The code reads top to bottom. In the Java version every stage names its executor, and whatever you chain next runs where the last stage left off, not back where you started.

withContext is also a scope, like coroutineScope in lesson 3 of this track. It waits for any children launched inside the block, and a failure inside it comes out as an exception in the caller.

A switch is cheap but not free: the library queues a task on the other dispatcher, and the coroutine's state machine resumes there. Values you wrote before the switch are visible after it, even on another thread. The library provides that happens-before edge, so you don't need @Volatile for a coroutine's own locals.

try.title: Print where each step runs
steps: Read WhereDoesItRun.kt. It turns on debug mode, which adds the coroutine's name and number to thread names. Predict the thread for each line.
Run it. Look closely at the two Unconfined lines.
Run it two or three times. Do Default and IO always print different workers?
Run the Java twin and match each line to its Kotlin counterpart.

code.title: WhereDoesItRun.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors private fun here() = Thread.currentThread().toString() fun main() { // debug mode adds " @name#id" to thread names. Set it before any coroutine starts. System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug", "on") runBlocking(CoroutineName("statement")) { println("runBlocking ${here()}") withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { println("Default ${here()}") } withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("IO ${here()}") } withContext(Dispatchers.Unconfined) { println("Unconfined, before ${here()}") delay(10) // resumes on whatever thread finishes the delay println("Unconfined, after ${here()}") } Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "ledger-writer") }.asCoroutineDispatcher().use { single -> withContext(single + CoroutineName("ledger")) { println("single-thread exec ${here()}") } } Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> withContext(vt) { println("virtual-thread exec ${here()}") } } } }

alt.title: WhereDoesItRunJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of WhereDoesItRun.kt: in Java you pick an executor for each step yourself. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class WhereDoesItRunJava { static String here() { return Thread.currentThread().toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("main " + here()); // the common pool: one thread per core, the closest match for Dispatchers.Default CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("commonPool " + here()), ForkJoinPool.commonPool()).join(); // a cached pool grows for blocking work, roughly what Dispatchers.IO does (without the cap) ExecutorService cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("cached pool " + here()), cached).join(); cached.shutdown(); // a non-async stage runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage, like Unconfined CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 1, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) .thenAccept(x -> System.out.println("thenAccept after timer " + here())) .join(); try (ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "ledger-writer"))) { CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("single-thread exec " + here()), single).join(); } try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("virtual-thread exec " + here()), vt).join(); } } }

try.expect: runBlocking prints main @statement#1. Default and IO print DefaultDispatcher-worker-N threads, and on some runs IO prints the same worker as Default: the two share one pool. Unconfined starts on main and, after delay, resumes on kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor, the thread that fired the timer. The single-thread executor prints ledger-writer @ledger#1 (the new name replaced the old one) and the virtual-thread executor prints a VirtualThread. In the Java twin, the thenAccept stage runs on whichever thread completed the timer stage, which is Java's version of Unconfined.

sections.h: Default is for CPU work, IO is for blocking calls
sections.html:
Dispatchers.Default has as many threads as the machine has cores. On a 4-core pod that is 4. Run a 200 ms blocking query there and you hold one of those 4 threads for 200 ms while it does nothing. Four requests doing that at once take every thread, and all the CPU work in the service waits in the queue: JSON parsing, signature checks, and the coroutines of every other request.

A blocking call belongs on Dispatchers.IO. Its limit is 64 (or the number of cores, if that is larger), set by the system property kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism. IO threads spend most of their time asleep in the kernel, waiting for Oracle or the issuer to answer, so 64 of them on 4 cores is fine.

IO and Default share one pool of worker threads. When code on Default calls withContext(Dispatchers.IO), the docs say it "typically does not lead to an actual switching to another thread": the same worker keeps going, and the library counts it against IO's limit instead of Default's. What the split buys you is separate budgets. Blocking work can fill IO, and Default still has a thread for every core.

Three rules follow.

Never block on Default. Put withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around each blocking call at the lowest level, inside the repository or the client, so callers don't need to know the call blocks.

Put long CPU work on Default: laying out a statement PDF, hashing a file of card numbers. A few microseconds of CPU work need no switch at all.

Don't wrap calls that already suspend. A non-blocking HTTP client, a delay or a Channel.receive never holds a thread while waiting, so withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around them only adds a hop.

The Java world has the same split under other names. The common ForkJoinPool is sized for CPU work, and blocking in it starves parallelStream() and every CompletableFuture.supplyAsync without an executor. Lesson 3 of the executors track sized a pool for each kind of work. Here the library gives you the two pools ready-made, and your job is to put each call in the right one.

try.title: Starve Default with blocking calls
steps: Read BlockingOnDefault.kt. It starts 32 blocking calls of 200 ms, then asks Default to run a task that takes a microsecond. Predict how long that tiny task waits to start on your machine.
Run it.
Run it with -Pargs=io, which puts the blocking calls on IO. Predict first.
Run the Java twin both ways.

code.title: BlockingOnDefault.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** 32 blocking 200 ms calls, then one tiny CPU task on Default. Pass "io" to run the blocking calls on IO. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val onIo = args.firstOrNull() == "io" val blockingDispatcher = if (onIo) Dispatchers.IO else Dispatchers.Default val cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() var cpuWaitMs = 0L val took = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(32) { launch(blockingDispatcher) { Thread.sleep(200) } } // JDBC-style blocking calls delay(20) // let them start val asked = System.nanoTime() val heartbeat = async(Dispatchers.Default) { System.nanoTime() } // 1 microsecond of CPU work cpuWaitMs = (heartbeat.await() - asked) / 1_000_000 } } val where = if (onIo) "Dispatchers.IO" else "Dispatchers.Default" println("32 blocking calls on $where ($cores cores): $took ms") println("a tiny CPU task on Default waited $cpuWaitMs ms to start") }

alt.title: BlockingOnDefaultJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of BlockingOnDefault.kt: blocking calls on the common pool (sized for CPU work) // versus on a separate pool for blocking work. Pass "io" to use the separate pool. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; public class BlockingOnDefaultJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean onIo = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("io"); int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64); // a pool sized like the common pool, so the demo behaves the same on every machine ForkJoinPool cpu = new ForkJoinPool(Math.max(2, cores)); var blockingPool = onIo ? io : cpu; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) { calls.add(CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> sleep(200), blockingPool)); // JDBC-style blocking calls } Thread.sleep(20); long asked = System.nanoTime(); long started = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(System::nanoTime, cpu).join(); // tiny CPU task on the CPU pool CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); System.out.printf("32 blocking calls on %s (%d cores): %d ms%n", onIo ? "a 64-thread pool" : "the CPU pool", cores, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); System.out.printf("a tiny CPU task on the CPU pool waited %d ms to start%n", (started - asked) / 1_000_000); io.shutdown(); cpu.shutdown(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: On 4 cores, the 32 calls take about 1,600 ms on Default (8 rounds of 4) and the tiny task waits about 1,500 ms, because every Default thread is asleep in Thread.sleep. With -Pargs=io the calls take about 220 ms (all 32 at once) and the tiny task starts within a few milliseconds. Scale the numbers to your core count. The Java twin shows the same starvation with a ForkJoinPool sized like Default.

sections.h: A limitedParallelism view gives each resource its own budget
sections.html:
IO's 64 is one budget for every blocking call in the JVM. That hurts when one resource is slow. Say the card issuer's client blocks, and its connection pool has 20 connections. When the issuer slows down, 64 coroutines can pile into issuer calls: 20 hold a connection, 44 hold an IO thread while they wait for one, and the ledger's JDBC calls, which need IO threads too, queue behind them.

limitedParallelism makes a view of a dispatcher with its own limit:

Java
// Java equivalent: a separate pool per resource (a bulkhead)
ExecutorService issuer = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofPlatform().name("issuer-", 0).factory());
ExecutorService reports = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100, Thread.ofPlatform().name("reports-", 0).factory());
Kotlin
val issuer = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "issuer")     // at most 20 issuer calls at once
val reports = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(100, "reports")  // a batch export with its own budget

A view owns no threads and needs no closing. It is a gate in front of its parent: at most 20 coroutines from the issuer view run at the same moment, and the rest wait in the view's queue without holding a thread. The name is optional. It arrived in kotlinx.coroutines 1.9, when the API became stable, and it is what toString() returns, which helps in logs.

Views over IO are elastic: they don't take a share of IO's 64, they add to it. The KDoc's own example has a view of 100 for MySQL and one of 60 for MongoDB, and says the system may then run up to 64 + 100 + 60 blocking tasks at peak. So the view isolates the issuer both ways. It can't take more than 20 threads, and a burst of other IO work can't starve it either.

Views over Default are different. A view can never exceed its parent's parallelism, so Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(100) still runs at most one task per core. And limitedParallelism(1) gives you a view that runs one task at a time, which is not the same as a lock. Lesson 10 of this track shows why.

When you need a dispatcher that is not one of these, wrap an executor: executor.asCoroutineDispatcher(). That includes the virtual-thread executor from the virtual threads track, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher(). kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 has no built-in virtual-thread dispatcher, so this is the supported route. A wrapped executor is yours to close: the dispatcher is AutoCloseable, and close() shuts the executor down.

try.title: Three budgets for 400 blocking calls
steps: Read BlockingBudgets.kt. It runs 400 blocking calls of 200 ms on plain IO, on a view of 400 over IO, and on a virtual-thread executor. Predict the time and the peak for each.
Run it.
Change the view to Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(400) and run it again. Predict first.
Run the Java twin.

code.title: BlockingBudgets.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** 400 blocking calls of 200 ms each, on three different dispatchers. */ suspend fun runBlockingCalls(label: String, dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) { val active = AtomicInteger() val peak = AtomicInteger() val took = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(400) { launch(dispatcher) { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) Thread.sleep(200) // a blocking issuer call active.decrementAndGet() } } } } println("%-32s %5d ms, peak %3d calls at once".format(label, took, peak.get())) } fun main() = runBlocking { runBlockingCalls("Dispatchers.IO", Dispatchers.IO) runBlockingCalls("IO.limitedParallelism(400)", Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(400)) Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> runBlockingCalls("virtual-thread executor", vt) } }

alt.title: BlockingBudgetsJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of BlockingBudgets.kt: the same 400 blocking calls on a 64-thread pool, // a pool that grows as needed, and one virtual thread per call. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class BlockingBudgetsJava { static void runBlockingCalls(String label, ExecutorService pool) { AtomicInteger active = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (pool) { // close() waits for all 400 calls for (int i = 0; i < 400; i++) { pool.submit(() -> { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } // a blocking issuer call active.decrementAndGet(); }); } } System.out.printf("%-32s %5d ms, peak %3d calls at once%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, peak.get()); } public static void main(String[] args) { runBlockingCalls("fixed pool of 64", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64)); runBlockingCalls("cached pool (grows)", Executors.newCachedThreadPool()); runBlockingCalls("virtual thread per task", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()); } }

try.expect: Plain IO peaks at 64 calls at once, so 400 calls take 7 rounds, about 1,400 ms. The view of 400 runs all 400 at once in about 300 ms: it adds to IO's 64 instead of sharing it. The virtual-thread executor also peaks at 400. The view over Default peaks at your core count (at least 2) and takes far longer (about 20 s on 4 cores), because a view can't exceed its parent. The Java twin shows the same pattern with a fixed pool of 64, a cached pool and a virtual thread per task.

sections.h: The context is a set of elements, and + merges them
sections.html:
A coroutine context is a small immutable set of elements, at most one per key. You've met most of them already: the Job (the node in the tree from lesson 3 of this track), the dispatcher, CoroutineName, and CoroutineExceptionHandler (lesson 6). + combines two contexts, and when both have an element with the same key, the right side wins.

val ctx = Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("capture")
val renamed = ctx + CoroutineName("refund")
renamed[CoroutineName]             // CoroutineName(refund): the right side won
renamed[ContinuationInterceptor]   // Dispatchers.IO: untouched

A new coroutine's context is built in three steps: the scope's context, then the context you pass to the builder (which overrides it), then a fresh Job that is a child of the scope's job. So children inherit the dispatcher, the name and anything else you add, but every child gets its own job. withContext(ctx) builds the context of its block the same way.

Inside a suspend function, read an element with currentCoroutineContext()[Key]. The key is usually the element's companion object, which is why ctx[CoroutineName] reads so naturally. One change in kotlinx.coroutines 1.11: using CoroutineDispatcher as the key is deprecated, and later versions will reject it. Look the dispatcher up with ContinuationInterceptor.

You can define your own element by extending AbstractCoroutineContextElement and giving it a companion Key. The lab does that to carry a payment's trace id into every coroutine that works on the payment.

What does not follow a coroutine is a plain ThreadLocal. A coroutine that resumes on another thread sees that thread's value, which is how request ids and MDC log fields go missing after a withContext. asContextElement() turns a ThreadLocal into an element. The library sets the value on whichever thread runs the coroutine and restores the old value when the coroutine leaves.

Java
// Java equivalent: copy the ThreadLocal into the task by hand
String captured = REQUEST_ID.get();
pool.submit(() -> {
    REQUEST_ID.set(captured);
    try { work(); } finally { REQUEST_ID.remove(); }
});
Kotlin
requestId.set("req-42")
withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { requestId.get() }                                // null: another thread
withContext(Dispatchers.Default + requestId.asContextElement()) { requestId.get() }  // req-42

For SLF4J's MDC there is a ready-made element, MDCContext, in the kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j module, which is not on this lab's classpath. And CoroutineName shows up in thread names when the JVM runs with -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug (assertions with -ea turn it on too). That costs little, and it makes thread dumps readable.

try.title: Merge contexts and lose a ThreadLocal
steps: Read ContextElements.kt. Predict the three lines about requestId.
Run it.
Add + CoroutineName("late") to the end of the renamed line and run again. Which name wins now?

code.title: ContextElements.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asContextElement import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlin.coroutines.ContinuationInterceptor private val requestId = ThreadLocal<String?>() fun main() = runBlocking { // 1. a context is a set of elements; + combines them, and the right side wins for the same key val ctx = Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("capture") val renamed = ctx + CoroutineName("refund") println("ctx[CoroutineName] = ${ctx[CoroutineName]}") println("renamed[CoroutineName] = ${renamed[CoroutineName]}") println("dispatcher by its key = ${renamed[ContinuationInterceptor]}") // 2. a ThreadLocal does not follow a coroutine to another thread requestId.set("req-42") println("main thread sees ${requestId.get()}") withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { println("on Default, plain ThreadLocal ${requestId.get()}") } // 3. asContextElement copies the value in and out whenever the coroutine runs on a thread withContext(Dispatchers.Default + requestId.asContextElement()) { println("on Default, asContextElement ${requestId.get()}") } }

alt.title: ContextElementsJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ContextElements.kt: a ThreadLocal does not follow a task to a pool thread. // You copy it by hand (this is what MDC-propagating executor wrappers do). JDK 25 adds ScopedValue // (final in JDK 25, JEP 506), but the labs compile for Java 21, so this demo copies by hand. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class ContextElementsJava { static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>(); // capture the caller's value now, install it around the task later, then restore static Runnable withRequestId(Runnable task) { String captured = REQUEST_ID.get(); return () -> { String previous = REQUEST_ID.get(); REQUEST_ID.set(captured); try { task.run(); } finally { REQUEST_ID.set(previous); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) { REQUEST_ID.set("req-42"); System.out.println("main thread sees " + REQUEST_ID.get()); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("pool thread, plain ThreadLocal " + REQUEST_ID.get()), pool).join(); CompletableFuture.runAsync(withRequestId(() -> System.out.println("pool thread, copied by hand " + REQUEST_ID.get())), pool).join(); } } }

try.expect: The name lookups print CoroutineName(capture), then CoroutineName(refund), and the dispatcher lookup prints Dispatchers.IO. The main thread sees req-42, the plain ThreadLocal on Default prints null, and the asContextElement version prints req-42. After your change the rightmost name, late, wins. The Java twin prints the same three requestId lines.

analogy: A dispatcher is the dispatch desk at a delivery company. Default is a small team of in-house drivers, one per loading bay, who never sit idle. IO is a large pool of contract drivers who spend most of the day parked outside customers' buildings, waiting for someone to sign. A limitedParallelism view is a separate contract for one difficult customer: at most 20 drivers on that route, hired on top of the usual pool. The context is the delivery note stapled to each parcel: which desk, which customer, which tracking number, and every parcel split off from it gets a copy. The analogy breaks on idle drivers. A real driver waiting at a door can't be reassigned. A suspended coroutine gives its thread back at once, which is why only blocking calls need the IO desk at all.
world: In a Quarkus service, coroutines usually start on a worker or event-loop thread and then run wherever their dispatcher sends them. Give each blocking dependency a view sized to its real limit: Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "oracle") for an Agroal pool of 20 connections, and another for a blocking issuer SDK. Then a slow issuer can't take the threads the ledger queries need. Wrap the JDBC call itself in withContext(oracle) inside the repository, so a Kafka consumer coroutine on Default never blocks on Oracle. And if your logs rely on an MDC trace id, carry it in the context (MDCContext or asContextElement). Otherwise the half of a payment's log lines written after the first withContext will be missing it.
mistake: The most common mistake is a blocking call on Default: a JDBC query, a blocking HTTP client, a Thread.sleep in a retry loop, inside a launch that inherited Default. It works in tests with one request at a time and falls over under load, when a handful of slow queries occupy every core's thread. People make it because nothing in the type system marks a call as blocking, and the code looks like any other function call. Wrap every blocking call in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) (or a view sized to the resource) inside the function that makes it, so the caller can't get it wrong. The opposite mistake is cheaper but still common: wrapping already-suspending calls in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) "to be safe", which adds a hop and hides which calls really block.

compare.title: One request, two kinds of work: executors vs dispatchers

java.title: StatementService.java
java.html: class StatementService { private final ExecutorService io; // sized for blocking JDBC calls private final ExecutorService cpu; // sized to the cores StatementService(ExecutorService io, ExecutorService cpu) { this.io = io; this.cpu = cpu; } CompletableFuture<byte[]> statementPdf(String accountId) { return CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() -> store.loadRows(accountId), io) // 1. block on an IO thread .thenApplyAsync(renderer::render, cpu); // 2. render on a CPU thread // the caller gets a future; whatever it chains next runs on a cpu thread } }

kotlin.title: StatementService.kt
kotlin.html: class StatementService( private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO, private val cpu: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default, ) { suspend fun statementPdf(accountId: String): ByteArray { val rows = withContext(io) { store.loadRows(accountId) } // 1. block on an IO thread return withContext(cpu) { renderer.render(rows) } // 2. render on a CPU thread } // the caller resumes on its own dispatcher with the bytes }

compare.note: Both versions keep the blocking call off the CPU threads, and both take the pools as constructor arguments so a test can pass its own. The difference is where the caller ends up. With CompletableFuture, the result is delivered on the thread of the last stage, and the caller either blocks on join() or keeps chaining callbacks that run who knows where. With withContext, the caller suspends, and when the block finishes it resumes on its own dispatcher, as if the call had been ordinary. You also own less: Dispatchers.IO and Dispatchers.Default are shared, process-wide pools that you never create or shut down, while the Java version needs two executors with a lifecycle.

worked.title: Give a blocking issuer client a budget of its own

steps.say: A Kafka consumer captures card payments with a blocking issuer SDK. Each record is handled in launch on Default, on a 4-core pod. When the issuer slows to 2 s per call, consumer lag climbs and unrelated CPU work in the pod stalls.
steps.code: class CaptureHandler(private val issuer: BlockingIssuerClient, private val scope: CoroutineScope) { fun onRecord(record: CaptureRequest) { scope.launch { // scope uses Dispatchers.Default val result = issuer.capture(record) // blocks a Default thread for up to 2 s ledger.record(result) } } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the bug: blocking calls on the common pool, which is sized for CPU work class CaptureHandler { void onRecord(CaptureRequest record) { CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> issuer.capture(record)) // no executor: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() .thenAccept(ledger::record); } }

steps.say: First, get the blocking call off Default. Put the switch inside a small suspend wrapper around the SDK, so no caller can forget it.
steps.code: class SuspendingIssuer(private val sdk: BlockingIssuerClient) { // 1. the only place that knows this SDK blocks suspend fun capture(req: CaptureRequest): CaptureResult = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { sdk.capture(req) } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: the wrapper picks the executor, so callers can't forget class AsyncIssuer { private final ExecutorService io = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // 1. the only place that knows this SDK blocks CompletableFuture<CaptureResult> capture(CaptureRequest req) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sdk.capture(req), io); } }

steps.say: IO allows 64 calls, but the SDK's pool has 20 connections. A slow issuer would let 64 coroutines take IO threads, and 44 of them would only be waiting for a connection, while ledger queries queue for IO threads. Give the issuer a view sized to its pool, and inject it so a test can pass a test dispatcher.
steps.code: class SuspendingIssuer( private val sdk: BlockingIssuerClient, // 2. a budget sized to the SDK's 20 connections, on top of IO's 64 private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "issuer"), ) { suspend fun capture(req: CaptureRequest): CaptureResult = withContext(dispatcher) { sdk.capture(req) } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: a bulkhead pool of exactly 20 threads for the issuer class AsyncIssuer implements AutoCloseable { // 2. a budget sized to the SDK's 20 connections private final ExecutorService issuerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofPlatform().name("issuer-", 0).factory()); CompletableFuture<CaptureResult> capture(CaptureRequest req) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sdk.capture(req), issuerPool); } @Override public void close() { issuerPool.shutdown(); } }

steps.say: The handler no longer cares where the issuer runs. Its own work (mapping, a suspending ledger call) can stay on Default.
steps.code: fun onRecord(record: CaptureRequest) { scope.launch { val result = issuer.capture(record) // 3. suspends; no Default thread is held ledger.record(result) // back on Default } }

alt.html: void onRecord(CaptureRequest record) { issuer.capture(record) // 3. runs on the issuer pool .thenAccept(ledger::record); // and so does this stage, unless you pass an executor }

steps.say: Self-check: why not Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20).asCoroutineDispatcher() instead of the view? (It works, but it is a pool you must close, with 20 threads that sit idle between bursts. The view has no lifecycle, borrows threads from the shared pool only while calls run, and still caps the issuer at 20.)

lab.title: Put each call on the right dispatcher
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. Read StatementModel.kt first: it has the blocking store, the CPU renderer and a PaymentTrace context element.

In StatementService.statementPdf, run loadRows inside withContext(io) and render inside withContext(cpu). The tests pass two single-thread dispatchers named test-io and test-cpu, so they can see where each call ran.
Write issuerDispatcher(): a view over Dispatchers.IO that allows exactly 20 calls at once and is named issuer. Don't create a thread pool.
Write withPaymentTrace: run the block in withContext with a PaymentTrace(traceId) and a CoroutineName("payment-$traceId"), combined with +.
Write currentTraceId(): read the PaymentTrace element from the current context by its key.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: withContext(io) { store.loadRows(accountId) } returns the rows. You don't need async, because the two steps depend on each other.
limitedParallelism takes an optional second argument, the view's name. The name is what toString() returns.
withContext(context, block) accepts the block parameter as it is. PaymentTrace(id) + CoroutineName("payment-$id") is a CoroutineContext.
currentCoroutineContext() (from kotlinx.coroutines) returns the context of the calling coroutine. The companion object PaymentTrace is the key, so ctx[PaymentTrace] gives you a PaymentTrace?.

drill.title: Two dispatchers and a budget, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write suspend fun riskReport(merchantId: String): Report that loads transactions with a blocking repo.load(merchantId) and scores them with a CPU-heavy scorer.score(rows), each on the right dispatcher. Then declare a dispatcher for a blocking sanctions-screening client that has a pool of 8 connections, without creating a thread pool.

answer.html: suspend fun riskReport(merchantId: String): Report { val rows = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { repo.load(merchantId) } // blocking: IO return withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { scorer.score(rows) } // CPU: Default } val sanctions: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(8, "sanctions")

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: one executor per kind of work, plus a bulkhead pool CompletableFuture<Report> riskReport(String merchantId) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> repo.load(merchantId), ioPool) // blocking: IO pool .thenApplyAsync(scorer::score, cpuPool); // CPU: CPU pool } ExecutorService sanctions = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, Thread.ofPlatform().name("sanctions-", 0).factory());

recap: The dispatcher in a coroutine's context picks its thread. launch and async default to Dispatchers.Default, which has one thread per core (at least 2).
Blocking calls go on Dispatchers.IO (64 at once by default), wrapped in withContext inside the function that blocks. CPU work goes on Default. Calls that already suspend need no switch.
withContext runs a block on another dispatcher and resumes the caller on its own, with the result. IO and Default share threads, so the switch is cheap.
Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n, name) is a budget for one resource. IO views add to the 64, while views over Default never exceed the core count.
A context is a set of elements keyed by type. + merges them, with the right side winning, and children inherit everything except the Job.
A plain ThreadLocal does not follow a coroutine across threads. Carry it with asContextElement() (or MDCContext for logging).

explain.prompt: A teammate's payment-status endpoint got slow under load, and so did unrelated endpoints. You find repo.findStatus(id), a blocking JDBC call, inside a coroutine on Default. Explain what was happening and the two changes you would make.
explain.answer: Default has one thread per core, so on our 4-core pods only 4 coroutines can run on it at once. The JDBC call doesn't suspend, it blocks, so each slow query held a Default thread for its whole duration. A few slow queries took every Default thread, and all the CPU work in the service, including other endpoints, waited in the queue. First, I'd wrap the call in withContext inside the repository, so it runs on IO and nobody calling findStatus has to remember. Second, I'd give the database its own budget, Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "oracle") to match our 20-connection pool, so a slow Oracle can't use up IO threads that other blocking calls need. That view adds to IO's 64 rather than taking from them, and it needs no closing.

deeper.html:
Default and IO are two faces of one scheduler. On the JVM, kotlinx.coroutines runs a single pool of worker threads, and each task is marked as CPU work or blocking work. A worker running a blocking task doesn't count against Default's limit, so the scheduler can start another worker for CPU work. That is how a switch from Default to IO can stay on the same thread: the worker just changes which budget it is counted against. IO itself is a view of 64 over an unbounded blocking budget, which is why further views over IO can add to it.

The docs say Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) can safely replace the older newFixedThreadPoolContext(n). The old function creates n dedicated threads that you must close, and that idle between bursts. If you find it in a codebase, a view is almost always the better choice.

Dispatchers.Unconfined has one legitimate niche: code that must react immediately on whatever thread delivered an event, such as some operator internals. To avoid stack overflows, nested unconfined coroutines form an event loop instead of calling each other recursively, which makes the order of execution surprising. Treat it as a library-writer's tool.

A virtual-thread dispatcher (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()) is an interesting option for code that blocks a lot, because each task gets a cheap virtual thread instead of an IO worker. It is not a free win. A virtual thread pinned by synchronized on JDK 21 to 23 (JEP 491 removed most pinning in JDK 24) still holds a carrier. Every time the coroutine resumes, the executor starts a new virtual thread for it, so you lose the scheduler's habit of keeping a coroutine on the same worker. And cancelling a coroutine blocked inside it still needs runInterruptible, which lesson 5 of this track covers. Lesson 11 of this track compares the options for a whole service.
